revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Car Sales
revealWordProblem.text: A dealership sold 50 cars last month: 20 sedans, 15 SUVs, 10 trucks, and 5 vans. The owner needs to order 50 cars from the factory for next month. Based on these sales, write each type as a percent and recommend how many of each type to order.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Rewrite each count as a ratio out of 100. Multiplying both terms by 2: sedans 20/50 = 40%, SUVs 15/50 = 30%, trucks 10/50 = 20%, vans 5/50 = 10%. The percents add to 100%, so the whole month is accounted for. Applying those percents to an order of 50 cars: 40% of 50 = 20 sedans, 30% of 50 = 15 SUVs, 20% of 50 = 10 trucks, and 10% of 50 = 5 vans. Because the order size matches last month's total, the recommended order matches last month's sales exactly — but stating it in percents means the same recommendation would work for an order of any size.

conceptIntro.heading: What a percent really says
conceptIntro.intro: Percent means per hundred. Any part-to-whole comparison becomes a percent by rewriting it as an equivalent ratio whose second term is 100. A decimal grid makes that visible: 100 squares, one for each percent.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Understanding Percent. Formula: Percent = Parts per 100 = Ratio of a number to 100. 1. Percent means 'per hundred' (% = /100). 2. On a 100-grid, each square represents 1% = 0.01 = 1/100. 3. Fraction to Percent: Scale fraction to a denominator of 100

iDo.title: Watch me turn a vote into a percent
lines: Students voted on a mascot, and 4 out of every 10 voters chose the tiger. I want to know how many that is out of 100.
"4 out of every 10" is a ratio, so I write an equivalent ratio with 100 as the second term. Multiplying both terms by 10 gives 40 out of 100.
On a decimal grid of 100 squares, I shade 40 squares — one square for each percent.
40 out of 100 is written 40%. So 40% of the students voted for the tiger.
linesEs: Los estudiantes votaron por una mascota, y 4 de cada 10 votantes eligieron al tigre. Quiero saber cuántos son de cada 100.
«4 de cada 10» es una razón, así que escribo una razón equivalente con 100 como segundo término. Multiplicar los dos términos por 10 da 40 de cada 100.
En una cuadrícula decimal de 100 cuadros, sombreo 40 cuadros — un cuadro por cada porcentaje.
40 de cada 100 se escribe 40%. Entonces el 40% de los estudiantes votó por el tigre.
iDo.titleEs: Mírame convertir una votación en un porcentaje

weDo.title: Let's do one together
lines: Shanice's gray kitten weighs 4 ounces. The orange kitten weighs 1.5 times as much. What percent of the gray kitten's weight is the orange kitten's weight?
The gray kitten is the whole, so its weight is 100%.
Draw a tape diagram: one full tape is 100%. The orange kitten needs 1.5 tapes — one whole tape plus half of another.
One whole is 100% and half a whole is 50%, so 100% + 50% = 150%. The orange kitten weighs 150% of the gray kitten's weight — more than one whole, which matches it being the heavier kitten.
linesEs: El gatito gris de Shanice pesa 4 onzas. El gatito naranja pesa 1.5 veces eso. ¿Qué porcentaje del peso del gatito gris es el peso del gatito naranja?
El gatito gris es el entero, así que su peso es el 100%.
Dibuja un diagrama de barras: una barra completa es el 100%. El gatito naranja necesita 1.5 barras — una barra entera más la mitad de otra.
Un entero es 100% y medio entero es 50%, así que 100% + 50% = 150%. El gatito naranja pesa el 150% del peso del gatito gris — más de un entero, lo que concuerda con que sea el gatito más pesado.

conceptIntro.headingEs: Lo que de verdad dice un porcentaje
conceptIntro.introEs: Porcentaje significa por cada cien. Cualquier comparación de parte al todo se vuelve un porcentaje si la reescribes como una razón equivalente cuyo segundo término sea 100. Una cuadrícula decimal lo hace visible: 100 cuadros, uno por cada porcentaje.

En una cuadrícula de 100, cada cuadro representa 1% = 0.01 = 1/100. 3. De fracción a porcentaje: escala la fracción a un denominador de 100

extending.correctWork: Step 2 compares the percents instead of the amounts. Each percent applies to a different whole: 40% of 200 = 80, while 150% of 40 = 60. Since 80 > 60, the first amount is larger — even though its percent is smaller.
extending.explanation: A percent is meaningless until you know what it is a percent OF. A small percent of a big whole can easily beat a large percent of a small whole.

extending.explanationEs: Un porcentaje no significa nada hasta que sepas de QUÉ es porcentaje. Un porcentaje pequeño de un entero grande puede superar fácilmente a un porcentaje grande de un entero pequeño.

extending.stem: A car dealership sold 50 cars last month: 20 sedans, 15 SUVs, 10 trucks, and 5 vans. The owner will order 100 cars for next month and wants the order to match last month's sales pattern. Write each type as a percent, then say how many of each to order — and explain why percents make this easier than the raw counts.
extending.sampleAnswer: Each count is out of 50, so multiply both terms by 2 to compare to 100: sedans 20/50 = 40/100 = 40%, SUVs 15/50 = 30/100 = 30%, trucks 10/50 = 20/100 = 20%, vans 5/50 = 10/100 = 10%. The percents total 100%, which confirms the whole is accounted for. Because the new order is exactly 100 cars, each percent IS the number to order: 40 sedans, 30 SUVs, 20 trucks, and 10 vans. Percents make this easier because they restate every count against the same whole of 100, so two months with different totals can be compared directly.
hints: Each sale count is out of 50 — rewrite each one out of 100.
What do you multiply 50 by to get 100?

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake with percent is scaling only one term of the ratio: reading 7 out of 10 as 7%. A percent compares to 100, so BOTH terms must be multiplied by the same factor — 10 × 10 = 100, so 7 × 10 = 70, giving 70%. Reading it as 7% describes seats that are nearly empty when they are nearly full. A second mistake is treating a percent as an amount: 150% of a 200-point goal is 1.5 × 200 = 300 points, not 150 points.
